```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(scales)
library(csgjcr)
library(highcharter)
library(htmlwidgets)
library(reactable)

source("R/page-data.R")
source("R/utils.R")

# htmlwidgets seeds its element IDs from this, so rerenders give identical HTML
set.seed(2019)
```

```{r}
srs_state_new <- read_srs_state()
latest_year <- max(srs_state_new$year)
first_year <- latest_year - 10

### U.S. benchmarks match the national page: solve rates leave out the
### excluded states but apply to U.S. reported counts
srs_by_cat_us <- violent_totals(srs_state_new, first_year)
srs_us <- violent_by_offense(srs_state_new, first_year)
srs_by_cat_us_solve <- us_solve_trend(srs_state_new, first_year)
us_total <- total_rate_benchmark(srs_by_cat_us, base_year, latest_year, solves = srs_by_cat_us_solve)
us_solved_rate_latest <- us_solve_benchmark(srs_state_new, latest_year)
```

```{r}
### city police departments from the agency tables built by
### R/01-prep-agency-county-data.R
agency_table_all <- read_rds("data/agency_table.rds")
agency_year <- agency_table_all$agency_year[1]
agency_base_year <- agency_table_all$base_year[1]

### the city charts compare agency rates with the U.S. rates of the same year
if (agency_year != latest_year || agency_base_year != base_year) {
  stop("The agency tables use ", agency_base_year, " and ", agency_year, " but the page uses ",
       base_year, " and ", latest_year, ". Update the agency data and rerun ",
       "R/01-prep-agency-county-data.R.", call. = FALSE)
}

### large city police departments; see city_solve_rows()
city_rows <- city_solve_rows(agency_table_all, read_rds("data/agency_offense_table.rds"))
### each city's state rates, from the same state estimates as the state pages
city_state_rates <- state_city_benchmarks(srs_state_new, city_rows$state_abbr, latest_year)
city_long <- city_solve_long(city_rows, benchmarks = city_state_rates)
city_rows <- city_rows |>
  left_join(
    city_state_rates |> filter(offense == total_label) |> select(state_abbr, state_solve_change),
    by = "state_abbr"
  )
n_cities <- nrow(city_rows)
```

# Solved violent crime in major cities, `r agency_year`

```{r}
### U.S. solve rate and crime rate per 100k for an offense, or for all violent
### crime when offense is total_label
us_offense_rates <- offense_rate_benchmark(srs_us, latest_year)
offense_key <- function(offense) names(table_offenses)[table_offenses == offense]
us_city_solve_rate <- function(offense) {
  if (offense == total_label) us_total$solve_rate else us_solved_rate_latest[[offense_key(offense)]]
}
us_city_crime_rate <- function(offense) {
  if (offense == total_label) us_total$rate_100k else us_offense_rates[[offense_key(offense)]]
}

### chart wrappers that fill in the page's agency data, U.S. rates and year
city_bar_chart <- function(offense, title) {
  agency_solve_bar_chart(city_long, offense, us_city_solve_rate(offense), title, agency_year)
}
city_scatter <- function(offense, title) {
  agency_solve_scatter(city_long, offense, us_city_solve_rate(offense), us_city_crime_rate(offense),
                       title, agency_year)
}

n_cities_below <- agencies_below(city_long, total_label, us_total$solve_rate)

### rape solve rates depend on recording practices; the caveat on the rape tabs
### names the lowest and highest departments from the data
rape_rows <- filter(city_long, offense == "Rape", shown) |> arrange(solved_rate)
rape_example <- function(row) {
  paste0("the ", row$agency_name, " (", row$state_abbr, ") reported solving ", comma(row$n_solved),
         " of ", comma(row$n_reported), " rapes (", solve_rate_text(row$solved_rate), ")")
}
### sources for the rape caveat, also cited in the methodology
case_cleared_url <-"https://www.propublica.org/article/when-it-comes-to-rape-just-because-a-case-is-cleared-does-not-mean-solved"
rti_clearance_url <- "https://www.rti.org/publication/using-national-incident-based-reporting-system-data-assess-agency-differences-clearance"
walfield_url <- "https://www.ojp.gov/ncjrs/virtual-library/abstracts/when-cleared-rape-not-cleared-multilevel-study-arrest-and"
rape_caveat <- paste0(
  "Rape solve rates are the least comparable across departments. They depend heavily on how agencies ",
  "record clearances, such as how often they clear a case by exceptional means, for example when a ",
  "victim declines to take part in prosecution ([ProPublica and Reveal](", case_cleared_url,
  "){target=\"_parent\"}; [Scott, Strom and Planty](", rti_clearance_url, "){target=\"_parent\"}). ",
  "Read rates at both extremes with caution. In ", agency_year, ", ",
  rape_example(head(rape_rows, 1)), ", and ", rape_example(tail(rape_rows, 1)), "."
)

### departments with a higher violent crime rate and a lower solve rate than the U.S.
n_cities_high_low <- agency_chart_rows(city_long, total_label, us_total$solve_rate) |>
  filter(n_reported_rate > us_total$rate_100k, side == "below") |>
  nrow()

city_changes <- agency_change_rows(city_rows, agency_base_year, agency_year)
n_cities_rose <- sum(city_changes$side == "above")

city_dumbbell <- function(offense, title) {
  agency_state_dumbbell(city_long, offense, us_city_solve_rate(offense), title, agency_year)
}
above_state <- agencies_above_state(city_long, total_label, us_total$solve_rate)

### CSG regions, for the regional panels, which share axes so they compare
csg_regions <- read_csv("data/csg-regions.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(state_abbr = csg_state_convert(state_name, "name", "abbr")) |>
  select(state_abbr, csg_region)
city_long <- left_join(city_long, csg_regions, by = "state_abbr")
if (anyNA(city_long$csg_region)) stop("Some city agencies have no CSG region", call. = FALSE)
region_names <- sort(unique(city_long$csg_region))
region_rows <- filter(city_long, offense == total_label, shown)
region_x_max <- ceiling(max(region_rows$n_reported_rate) / 500) * 500
region_y_max <- solve_pct_max(solve_rate_percent(region_rows$solved_rate))
city_region_scatter <- function(region) {
  agency_region_scatter(city_long, region, us_total$solve_rate, us_total$rate_100k,
                        region_x_max, region_y_max, agency_year)
}
```

::: {.callout-note icon=false title="City police departments only"}
This page currently includes only city police departments, so it can compare trends across cities. Sheriffs' offices, county police departments and state police are left out for now, even where they serve at least `r comma(min_city_population)` residents.
:::

The following visuals compare `r n_cities` police departments that each serve at least `r comma(min_city_population)` residents and reported full data to the FBI in `r agency_year`. Violent crime solve rates among these departments ranged from `r agency_range_text(city_long, total_label)`, compared with `r solve_rate_text(us_total$solve_rate)` in the United States. Of these departments, `r n_cities_below` solved a smaller share of violent crime than the nation as a whole.

For more information, see the [data sources and methodology](#methodology) section below.

## Solve rates by agency

Each bar shows one department's solve rate. The diamond on each bar indicates the overall solve rate for each department's state and the dashed line marks the overall U.S. solve rate. Hover over each bar for more information.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Crime rates and solve rates

Each point is one law enforcement agency. Larger circles represent agencies that serve more residents. Agencies to the right of the vertical line have higher crime rates than the United States while agencies to the left of the line reported crime rates lower than the U.S. average. Agencies below the horizontal line have solve rates lower than the nationwide average while agencies above the line have solve rates higher than the U.S. average. Hover over each point to learn more about a given agency. In `r agency_year`, `r n_cities_high_low` of the `r n_cities` departments had both a higher violent crime rate and a lower violent crime solve rate than the United States as a whole.

## Solved by arrest or by exceptional means

```{r}
### outcome of each 2025 violent incident for the city police departments
### charted above, by offense, from the FBI's incident-level data; the file
### covers agencies of any type; see R/download-nibrs-clearance.R
nibrs_clearance <- read_csv(paste0("data/nibrs_clearance_", agency_year, ".csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
if (any(nibrs_clearance$year != agency_year)) stop("data/nibrs_clearance_", agency_year, ".csv has other years", call. = FALSE)
nibrs_clearance <- filter(nibrs_clearance, ori %in% city_rows$ori)

### departments whose incident data look partial; see min_nibrs_share
nibrs_partial <- nibrs_clearance |>
  filter(offense == total_label, n_incidents < min_nibrs_share * n_srs_reported) |>
  mutate(pct_of_srs = n_incidents / n_srs_reported * 100) |>
  arrange(desc(population))
nibrs_clearance <- filter(nibrs_clearance, !ori %in% nibrs_partial$ori)
n_nibrs_agencies <- nrow(clearance_rows(nibrs_clearance, total_label, "cleared"))
nibrs_median_pct <- with(filter(nibrs_clearance, offense == total_label), median(n_incidents / n_srs_reported) * 100)

### departments from the charts above with no NIBRS incidents, because they
### report to the FBI in summary form
nibrs_missing <- filter(city_rows, !ori %in% c(nibrs_clearance$ori, nibrs_partial$ori)) |>
  arrange(desc(population))

agency_list <- function(rows) {
  knitr::combine_words(paste0(rows$agency_name, " (", rows$state_abbr, ")"))
}
nibrs_missing_text <- if (nrow(nibrs_missing) == 0) "" else {
  paste0(" The ", agency_list(nibrs_missing), " did not report incident-level data.")
}
nibrs_partial_text <- if (nrow(nibrs_partial) == 0) "" else {
  paste0(" The ", agency_list(nibrs_partial), " are also left out because their incident data look incomplete: ",
         "they reported between ", round(min(nibrs_partial$pct_of_srs)), " and ",
         floor(max(nibrs_partial$pct_of_srs)), " percent as many violent incidents as the violent crimes in ",
         "their summary counts, below the ", round(min_nibrs_share * 100), " percent threshold used here. ",
         "For the typical department the share is ", round(nibrs_median_pct), " percent, because summary ",
         "counts record one crime per victim and incident counts record one per incident.")
}

nibrs_clearance_chart <- function(offense, title) {
  clearance_chart(nibrs_clearance, offense, "cleared", title, agency_year)
}
### the sentence above each tab's chart; plural is the offense in the plural
nibrs_clearance_text <- function(offense, plural) {
  rows <- clearance_rows(nibrs_clearance, offense, "cleared")
  n_more <- sum(rows$n_exceptional > rows$n_arrest)
  paste0("Of the ", nrow(rows), " departments that recorded at least ", min_rate_reported, " ", plural,
         ", ", if (n_more == 0) "none" else n_more, " solved more ", plural,
         " by exceptional means than by arrest.")
}
```

The solve rates above count a crime as solved whether the agency solved it by arrest or by exceptional means. The FBI's incident-level data separate the two. The charts below use those data for `r n_nibrs_agencies` of the `r n_cities` police departments charted above.`r nibrs_missing_text``r nibrs_partial_text` Each offense tab includes the departments that recorded at least `r min_rate_reported` incidents of that offense in `r agency_year`.

A department's solve rate in these charts can differ from its solve rate above, because the two count different crimes. The solve rates above count every crime a department solved during `r agency_year`, including crimes committed in earlier years. These charts follow only crimes committed in `r agency_year`, each to its status when the FBI released the data. For example, a robbery committed in `r agency_year - 1` and solved in `r agency_year` counts as solved in the solve rates above but does not appear in these charts. A robbery committed in `r agency_year` and still unsolved when the FBI released the data counts as not solved here.

In each bar, `r clearance_outcome_color_text("arrest", "blue")` marks incidents solved by arrest, `r clearance_outcome_color_text("exceptional", "orange")` marks incidents solved by exceptional means, and `r clearance_outcome_color_text("not_cleared", "light blue")` marks incidents not solved. Hover over each bar for more information.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Solve rates by police department

The following tables list each department's crime rates and solve rates. Search by agency name or state to compare departments.

::: {.panel-tabset .column-body-outset}

### Overall rates

`r solve_rate_legend("below", "indicates a solve rate less than the U.S. rate.")`

`r solve_rate_legend("above", "indicates a solve rate greater than or equal to the U.S. rate.")`

[Gray solve rates and changes are based on fewer than `r min_rate_reported` reported incidents in a year.]{.small-n-note}

```{r}
city_rows |>
  select(agency_name, state_abbr, population, n_reported_rate, n_reported, solved_rate, solved_rate_change) |>
  reactable_template(
    sort_col = list("population" = "desc"),
    columnGroups = list(
      colGroup(name = paste("Violent crime,", agency_year),
               columns = c("n_reported_rate", "n_reported", "solved_rate")),
      colGroup(name = paste("Change since", agency_base_year), columns = "solved_rate_change")
    ),
    columns = list(
      agency_name = sticky_name_column("Agency", footer = "U.S. total"),
      state_abbr = colDef(name = "State", minWidth = 70),
      population = colDef(
        name = "Population", minWidth = table_widths$population,
        footer = comma(us_total$population)
      ),
      n_reported_rate = colDef(
        name = "Per 100k", cell = rate_100k_cell,
        footer = rate_100k_cell(us_total$rate_100k)
      ),
      n_reported = colDef(name = "Incidents", footer = comma(us_total$incidents)),
      solved_rate = solve_rate_column(
        us_total$solve_rate, reported = city_rows$n_reported, solved = city_rows$n_solved
      ),
      solved_rate_change = colDef(
        name = "Solve rate (points)",
        html = TRUE,
        footer = format_signed(us_total$solve_change),
        ### a change is as shaky as the smaller of its two years
        cell = small_n_cell(pmin(city_rows$n_reported, city_rows$n_reported_base), format_signed)
      )
    )
  )
```

[A dash (—) marks a solve-rate change left out because the department lacked full reporting in `r agency_base_year` or reported no violent crime or no solved crimes in `r agency_base_year`.]{.small-n-note}

::: {#methodology .callout-note icon=false collapse=true}

## Data sources and methodology

Data on crime and solve rates come from the FBI's [Uniform Crime Reporting Program](https://www.fbi.gov/how-we-can-help-you/need-an-fbi-service-or-more-information/ucr){target="_parent"}. Violent crime includes homicide, aggravated assault, robbery, and rape. Crime rates divide reported crimes by the population served.

{{< include _methodology-exceptional-clearance.qmd >}}

City solve rates come from the incidents each law enforcement agency reported to the FBI, available on the [Crime Data Explorer](https://cde.ucr.cjis.gov/LATEST/webapp/#/pages/downloads){target="_parent"}, rather than from the FBI's state estimates. The city charts and tables include agencies the FBI classifies as city agencies that served at least `r comma(min_city_population)` residents and reported all 12 months of `r agency_year`. Population is the number of residents the FBI counts in each agency's jurisdiction. Agencies that reported no violent crime or no solved crimes are left out. The Chicago Police Department is left out because Illinois did not report reliable clearance data. The St. Petersburg Police Department (FL) is left out because its `r agency_year` clearance data appear incomplete. Charts leave out an agency's rate for an offense when it rests on fewer than `r min_rate_reported` reported incidents. An agency's solve rate can exceed 100 percent when it solves incidents from earlier years. City rates are compared with U.S. and state rates from the state estimates, the same rates shown elsewhere on this site, and the change since `r agency_base_year` compares each agency with itself and needs full reporting in both years.

Regions follow the [CSG regional offices](https://www.csg.org/regional-offices){target="_parent"}.

Rape solve rates are the least comparable across departments. Agencies often clear rape cases by exceptional means, for example when a victim declines to take part in prosecution. A [2018 investigation by ProPublica](`r case_cleared_url`){target="_parent"} found that nearly half of the large police departments that provided data cleared more rapes by exceptional means than by arrest. Agencies differ in how often they do so, and that difference [explains most of the variation in sexual assault clearance rates across agencies](`r rti_clearance_url`){target="_parent"} (Scott, Strom and Planty, 2022; see also [Walfield, 2016](`r walfield_url`){target="_parent"}). The FBI agency data used for the solve rates do not separate clearances by arrest from exceptional clearances. In `r agency_year`, `r rape_example(head(rape_rows, 1))`, and `r rape_example(tail(rape_rows, 1))`. Such rates may reflect recording practices as much as how often cases are solved.

The charts that split solved crimes by arrest and exceptional means use the FBI's incident-level data from the National Incident-Based Reporting System (NIBRS), available by state on the [Crime Data Explorer](https://cde.ucr.cjis.gov/LATEST/webapp/#/pages/downloads){target="_parent"}. They count incidents in `r agency_year` that include a homicide (murder or nonnegligent manslaughter), rape (rape, sodomy, or sexual assault with an object, following the FBI's definition; fondling is not included), robbery, or aggravated assault. Following the hierarchy rule, each incident counts once, under its most serious offense, so the offense charts add up to the violent crime chart. An incident with an arrest counts as solved by arrest. An incident without one counts as solved by exceptional means when the agency recorded it that way, and as not solved otherwise. The charts include the city police departments in the charts above, except those that did not report incident-level data and those whose violent incident count was below `r round(min_nibrs_share * 100)` percent of their summary-count violent crimes, a sign of incomplete incident data; the section names them. Each offense chart leaves out departments with fewer than `r min_rate_reported` incidents of that offense. These data follow each `r agency_year` incident to its status when the FBI released the data, while the solve rates elsewhere on this page count crimes solved during `r agency_year`, including earlier crimes. The FBI's summary counts also record one homicide, rape, or aggravated assault for each victim, while these charts count incidents, so incident counts run lower than the reported counts elsewhere on this page, most of all for aggravated assault.

U.S. and state solve rates come from the FBI's state estimates, the same rates shown on the national and state pages. U.S. solve rates leave out `r knitr::combine_words(states_to_exclude_from_solved_rate_viz)`, which did not report reliable clearance data.

Crime counts follow the FBI's hierarchy rule, which counts only the most serious offense in each incident. Homicide ranks highest, followed by rape, robbery, and aggravated assault. An incident that includes both a robbery and an aggravated assault, for example, counts as one robbery.

:::
